content_voiceover: This diagram shows hemoglobin synthesis as two coordinated processes inside the erythroblast: iron delivery and heme biosynthesis. On the right, the transferrin cycle: transferrin receptor binds iron-loaded transferrin, it's endocytosed, iron drops into the cytoplasmic iron pool, and apo-transferrin recycles out. That iron pool does double duty, it feeds mitochondrial heme synthesis, and it stabilizes iron-sulfur clusters on IRE binding protein, which controls translation of ALAS-2, the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis. High iron favors ALAS-2 and globin mRNA translation together, keeping heme and globin production matched. The heme pathway itself, glycine plus B6 plus succinyl-CoA form delta-ALA, then porphobilinogen, then porphyrinogen intermediates, finishing in mitochondria where protoporphyrin plus ferrous iron makes heme. Four hemes combine with two alpha and two beta globin chains to form hemoglobin. High-yield point, ALAS-2 is iron- and erythropoietin-regulated and rate-limiting, defects anywhere in this pathway cause sideroblastic anemias or porphyrias, the topics of the next slides.
keypoints: ALAS-2 = rate-limiting, iron-regulated enzyme of heme synthesis
IRE-BP/Fe-S senses iron -> controls ALAS-2 mRNA translation
Pathway defects -> sideroblastic anemia or porphyria
keypoint_voiceover: The key takeaway, ALAS-2 is the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis, and it's controlled by iron availability through the IRE binding protein and iron-sulfur cluster system. This keeps heme production matched to both iron supply and globin chain synthesis. Remember that enzyme defects anywhere along this heme biosynthetic pathway lead to either sideroblastic anemia, when early steps in mitochondria are affected, or a porphyria, when later steps are affected.
